title: Coding agents can't hear a sound effect land 80 ms late
summary: Coding agents can't hear a sound effect land 80 ms late. earshot describes, scores and times audio in words an agent can use, and lets it synthesize sounds in code and refine them by listening: https://github.com/Leonxlnx/earshot
body_markdown:
Coding agents can now write the code that renders a product demo or a launch film, but they cannot hear what they made. They cannot tell a premium key press from a cheap one, notice a hit that lands 80 ms after the cut, or hear the music swell in the wrong place. earshot, from Leonxlnx/earshot, gives them ears by turning sound into evidence an agent can reason about.

It runs locally on CPU, as a CLI, a Python API and an MCP server.

## Sound, described in words an agent can use

The core commands answer the questions you would ask a sound designer:

```
$ earshot describe enter.ogg
  0.56 s short transient (attack 3 ms, decays in 190 ms). Sounds most like:
  a single mechanical keyboard key press (z +5.4) ...

$ earshot match key.ogg "a deep thocky mechanical keyboard press" --alts "a clicky blue switch keyboard" "a mouse click"
  strong (z +3.7; would rank #2 among 322 vocabulary descriptions) ...
```

`describe` returns calibrated tags with the closest alternative readings plus measurements. `match` scores how well a description fits and gives a verdict of strong, plausible, weak or no match. `find` locates the best moments in a long recording as start and end times. `realness` judges whether a file is a real or professionally produced recording or code-synthesized, with per-window scores.

For films, `timeline` produces a second-by-second listening transcript with events, loudness, a beat grid and the sync of sound to picture cuts. `sheet` renders an annotated PNG for agents that read images. `critique` scores a launch video against a profile of 7 professional launch films and returns timestamped fixes, like "nothing reaches body level until 0:01.01".

## Making sounds by listening to them

The part I find most interesting is `earshot forge`, where the agent writes a sound as code and improves it by listening. A recipe is physical synthesis: modal resonators, contact excitations, filtered noise, a computed room and a microphone, with no recorded audio inside.

The forge renders candidates from the recipe's parameters, and a critic built from earshot scores each one. It checks the description match against named confusions, realness, and closeness to real reference recordings. Model-free penalties cover tonal balance, a tail that dies too fast, artifacts such as clicks, aliasing and clipping, and polish such as attack and onset snap. A cheap pre-screen ranks many renders so the models only hear the best, and an evolutionary search keeps the winners and mutates them.

Then the agent reads the critic's words ("sounds like: a cork pop, a glass ting", "bumpy tail"), compares spectrograms with the references, rewrites the recipe and runs it again. Reference sets are split by source into a side the search may use and a side only the fixed benchmark hears. `earshot fit` runs the other direction and translates a recording into a recipe module that re-renders it, with knobs you can vary.

## A sound bank for code-made films

Version 0.3 added a bank of sound effects stored as code that render by id in seconds, with no models and no network. Version 0.4 brought it to 252 sounds, adding 51 aimed at the soft, short style of music-led launch films: UI pops, wood knocks, cut hits, glockenspiel notes, camera shutters and short risers. `earshot sfx` aims a whoosh or hit at a moment in the picture, and `earshot kit` renders a film's effects with measured sync points. The `launch` preset mixes effects against the music bed and places them against the cut, with taps leading it and whoosh peaks landing after it.

## Practical notes

Each CLI call is a new process and loads the models, which takes roughly 20 to 40 seconds before it answers. `measure`, `sfx` and `kit` load no models. For more than a few calls, the project points you to the MCP server, which keeps models loaded, or a single Python script using `from earshot import api`. Run `earshot doctor` to check the install.

There is an optional `llm` command that sends audio to Gemini, but only with your own key and explicit consent through a `--yes-upload` flag. The rest runs locally on CPU. If your agent already makes videos, I would run `earshot critique` on its last render and see which fix it lists first.
